title: Can American Schools Fuel Trump’s Manufacturing Revival?
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio asks whether American schools can actually produce the skilled workforce that Trump's manufacturing revival presumes. He treats Career and Technical Education as a comparative bright spot, citing research that CTE concentrators have better earnings and employment outcomes and are less likely to be disengaged. He then lays out the obstacles: CTE programs that do not match local labor markets, very few concentrators in manufacturing, difficulty hiring CTE teachers, and automation that raises the math and technical demands of factory work. The weak academic base, with only 26 percent of eighth-graders proficient in math, undercuts confidence that comprehensive high schools can deliver. He also notes that soft skills like initiative cannot be fixed by curriculum alone. His qualified maybe closes with a call for tighter CTE alignment, stronger academic foundations, and a culture that values work.
points: CTE is one of the few parts of K-12 that demonstrably connects students to jobs, with concentrators showing better earnings and lower poverty risk.
Misalignment with local labor markets and a thin manufacturing pipeline (about five percent of concentrators) weaken CTE's promise for a factory revival.
Automation turns manufacturing into robotics and CNC programming work, so weak middle-school math becomes a hard ceiling on technical careers.
Experts such as Shaun Dougherty find no evidence that comprehensive high schools teach CTE systematically better than they teach math and reading.
Initiative and work ethic matter to employers but are cultural traits that schools cannot manufacture through curriculum alone.
quotes: Does America’s education system have what it takes to produce the workforce needed to staff a manufacturing revival? To put the question bluntly, are we any better at Career and Technical Education (CTE) than teaching kids to read and do math proficiently?

Even more encouragingly, a 2022 report published by the Annenberg Institute at Brown University found CTE concentrators are 8.4 percentage points more likely to avoid poverty and are significantly more likely to earn above the poverty threshold seven years after high school. They are also less likely to be “disengaged,” i.e. neither employed nor participating in education or training.

Nothing useful comes from schools churning out workers trained as welders in regions where robotics or advanced manufacturing jobs dominate—or might in the future. More concerning, only about five percent of CTE concentrators focus on manufacturing, lagging behind other fields such as health science, agriculture, business management, and hospitality and tourism.

In sum, manufacturing isn’t what it used to be; it’s no longer about low-skill, repetitive tasks but about sophisticated, tech-driven processes. If three-quarters of our students can’t master middle school math, the demands of modern manufacturing are likely beyond them.

Taylor’s organization emphasizes mid-skill, mid-wage jobs as the goal—not low-skill, low-wage work that’s easily automated or offshored. But fostering the initiative to seize those opportunities requires more than curriculum; it demands a cultural shift.

We’ll need to fix the academic foundations—math, literacy, problem-solving—that underpin technical skills. And we’ll need to cultivate a culture that values hard work and opportunity, not just credentials.
